name: Aisha Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work a kilometre underground at a potash mine. Potash is a salt they use for fertiliser, and we cut it with a continuous miner, which is a long machine with big spinning cutting drums on the front. I run the miner and lead a crew of five, so I'm cutting the rooms, keeping an eye on the conveyor, and making sure the bolting crew is behind us keeping the roof safe. The hardest part is the noise and the salt dust, it gets into everything, even your lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Luis runs the hardware store on Centre Street, which his dad started. We own a duplex that we rent out to two young mining families, and both our daughters have moved to the city. I've been at the mine twenty-nine years. I'm good at it, and I'd like to finish in about four years and help Luis at the store a few days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, which is what I'd expect. Most new things at the mine turn out smaller than the people selling them say. I'd say it at the lunch table and to Luis, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the easiest picture for us. My job, the store, the rent from the duplex, all of it depends on the mine running like it does now. If nothing changes, we're set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to look up fault codes on the miner faster than the manual, and I'd carry on with that. I'd stay on track to retire in about four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the store and the duplex depend on the mine. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our tenants both work at the mine. Half of Luis's customers are miners doing jobs on their days off. If the mine sneezes, this whole town catches a cold, and we're right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI for fault codes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, our shift electrician, showed me. I waited until she'd been using it a year and it hadn't steered her wrong. Now I use it maybe twice a week, but I always double-check with the manual.

S0.say: I'd say it was overhyped, which I'd expect, since most new things at the mine turn out smaller than the sellers claim. I'd say it at lunch and to Luis.
S0.think: Privately it's the easiest picture for us, because my job, the store and the duplex rent all depend on the mine running as it does now. If nothing changes, we're set.
S0.do: Keeps working as now and uses an AI app a couple of times a week for fault codes, checking against the manual. Stays on track to retire in about four years.
S0.quote: If the mine sneezes, this whole town catches a cold, and we're right in the middle of it.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha's exposure is wider than her job: her husband's store and her rental tenants all rely on the mine. She adopted AI only after a colleague tested it for a year, which is typical of her careful approach. She talks like a practical household manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it depends how it's done. Some of it will make the job safer, some of it will cost people work. I'd say let's see the details before getting angry or excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job lasts, but the crew shrinks. They already run some miners partly by remote at another mine in the province. I'd probably go from leading five to leading three, and one of them would be a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the remote operation training once the first group had been through it and the bugs were out. I'd keep putting money aside like now. And I'd talk to Luis about the store, maybe stocking more for the farmers and less for the miners, just to spread things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some background worry about the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamal, the youngest. He's twenty-four and he only knows the miner. He's sharp, though. I'd push him to take the electrical course, because the machines will need more electricians, not fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the farmers. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's something Luis and I talk about. The farm trade is steadier than mining, they always need fencing wire and parts. It's not a big change, just a few more shelves.

S1.say: I'd say it depends how it's done, because some of it makes the job safer and some costs people work. I'd want to see the details before getting angry or excited.
S1.think: Privately I think my job lasts but the crew shrinks, probably from five to three with one run from a screen. Another mine in the province already runs some miners partly by remote.
S1.do: Signs up for remote operation training once the first group has been through it. Keeps saving as now and talks with Luis about stocking more farm supplies at the store to spread the risk.
S1.feel: Calm, with some background worry about the town.
S1.quote: I'd probably go from leading five to leading three, and one of them would be a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha thinks like someone managing a small portfolio: her job, the store and the rental. Her plan to shift the store towards farmers is modest and realistic. She mentors Jamal with concrete advice about electrical training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, not the companies, not the government, not us. I'd say we need to slow down and think. But I wouldn't be marching anywhere, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job matters less than the town. I'd be sixty and could stop. But if the mine goes robot in two years, our tenants lose their jobs, Luis loses half his customers, and the duplex is worth a lot less overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Luis that week about selling the duplex while it still has a good price, even if it means asking our tenants to find somewhere else, which I'd hate. I'd hold off on the kitchen renovation we'd planned. And I'd probably retire within the year rather than fight for a spot in the control room, and put my time into the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. We'd be fine, but we'd have to move fast, and I don't like moving fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the short timeline change things, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five or ten years, I could sell the duplex when I wanted, at a fair time. With two, I'm racing every other landlord in town. Everyone would have the same idea in the same month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask your tenants to leave. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. The Nguyens have been there six years, their boy's in the school band. I'd probably offer them first chance to buy it at a fair price, and give them plenty of time. It still wouldn't feel good.

S2.say: I'd say nobody's ready, not companies, government or workers, and we need to slow down and think. But I wouldn't be marching anywhere, that's not me.
S2.think: Privately my job matters less than the town, since I could stop at sixty. But our tenants would lose their jobs, Luis would lose half his customers and the duplex would lose value overnight.
S2.do: Discusses selling the duplex with Luis that week, offering the tenants first chance to buy. Holds off on the kitchen renovation and retires within the year to work at the store.
S2.feel: Anxious, because they'd be fine but would have to move fast, which she dislikes.
S2.quote: With two, I'm racing every other landlord in town. Everyone would have the same idea in the same month.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits Aisha through her assets rather than her pay. She would act quickly but felt real guilt about her tenants, the Nguyens. She separates what she would say publicly from protest, which isn't her style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to plan, so let's plan. The company should tell us its timetable, and the town council should be thinking about what comes after. I'd say that at a town meeting if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me just past retirement, so my job's not really at risk. It's the duplex and the store again, but with time to do it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the first mines that go fully automated for a year or two, then decide about the duplex, probably selling around 2029. I'd do the remote training if it was offered, since I'd still be working. And I'd help Luis build up the farm side of the store slowly over those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. I like having time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time buy you, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't have to race anyone. I can wait until I see it working at another mine, then act. That's how I do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your daughters anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older one, Sofia, is a nurse, and I'd tell her she's probably fine for a while. The younger one works in accounting, and that worries me more than the mine does, honestly. I'd tell her to start learning whatever tools are coming.

S3.say: I'd say we have time to plan, so let's plan, with the company sharing its timetable and the town council thinking about what comes after. I'd say it at a town meeting.
S3.think: Privately five years takes me past retirement, so my job isn't really at risk. It's the duplex and the store again, but with time to act calmly.
S3.do: Watches the first fully automated mines for a year or two, then likely sells the duplex around 2029. Takes remote training if offered and helps Luis slowly build up the farm side of the store.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in control, glad to have time.
S3.quote: I can wait until I see it working at another mine, then act. That's how I do everything.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Aisha returns to her natural pace of waiting for proof before acting. She revealed a worry that her younger daughter's accounting job is more exposed than her own mining work. She looks to the town council rather than national politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no excuse for the town not to be ready. I'd say the council and the company should start planning together. It's a practical thing, not a political one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my job, nothing. I'd be retired long before. For the store and the duplex, it's a slow change we can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire around sixty-two as planned. Over the years, I'd move some of our savings out of local property into something not tied to this town, maybe a fund the bank recommends. I'd keep the duplex for a while and see how the town is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still a little uneasy, if it's ten years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the town is our whole life. Luis's dad built that store. Even with ten years, I don't know what this place looks like if the mine runs itself, and nobody can tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to see the council do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start talking to the company now about what happens to the town. Maybe a processing plant, maybe something else. I don't know the answer, but I'd want to see someone asking the question.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so the town has no excuse not to be ready, and the council and company should plan together. It's practical, not political.
S4.think: Privately my job's fine because I'd be retired long before. For the store and the duplex it's a slow change we can manage.
S4.do: Retires around 62 as planned, and over the years moves some savings out of local property into an investment not tied to the town. Keeps the duplex for now and watches how the town fares.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly fine.
S4.quote: Even with ten years, I don't know what this place looks like if the mine runs itself, and nobody can tell me.
S4.fieldNote: Even ten years can't fully settle Aisha because her family's roots and assets are in one town. She is honest that she doesn't know what the town becomes. Her response is to spread her savings rather than to campaign.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to sell the duplex in a hurry and the store would lose half its customers at once. What would help is the company telling the town its timetable early, so families and businesses can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about people like us who own a bit of property in a mining town. Everybody thinks about the miners losing jobs. Nobody thinks about the house that's worth half what it was the next morning.

headlineQuote: Nobody thinks about the house that's worth half what it was the next morning.
portrait: Aisha Garcia is a 58-year-old continuous miner operator and crew lead at an underground potash mine, married to Luis, who runs the family hardware store, with a rental duplex let to mining families. She uses AI now and then for fault codes, but only after a colleague proved it, and she waits for proof before any change. Her job is safe in most pictures; what worries her is that the store, the rental and the town all depend on the mine. She is calm in the slower pictures and anxious in AGI by 2028, when she would have to sell the duplex in a hurry. She looks to the company and town council for planning, not to protest.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would have to sell the duplex in a hurry and the store would lose half its customers at once.
whatWouldHelp: The company sharing its automation timetable with the town early so families and businesses can plan.
